source.title: On the Optimal Weighted $\ell_2$ Regularization in Overparameterized Linear Regression

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some mathematical symbols are garbled by text extraction, but the relevant claims and results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes double-descent risk in linear regression, including principal component regression, rather than reproducing the original deep-network method. Its results also test whether risk improves beyond interpolation in other model classes.
record.gate_note: The paper explicitly analyzes double descent for PCR and reports risk curves for PCR and ridgeless regression. Its figures showing risk curves report no numeric curve values in the text. Results comparing ridge penalties or weighting matrices against λ are not rows because they measure regularization choices, not the claim versions' double-descent curves.
record.test_reason: The paper derives exact asymptotic risk for linear estimators, a non-deep model class. It shows a spike at the interpolation threshold with later descent for PCR (V4). It reports multiple peaks for ridgeless regression (V6) and monotone risk under optimally tuned ridge, i.e. no peak (V6, and V3 under tuning). Double descent is a secondary topic; the main subject is optimal weighted ridge.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the paraphrase misplaces the emphasis. The main conclusions concern exact asymptotic risk of generalized (weighted) ridge, conditions for a negative optimal ridge (implicit regularization of overparameterization), and the optimal weighting matrix (Σβ^-1 under optimal tuning). Double descent for PCR under anisotropic settings is a secondary result. Multiple descent of ridgeless risk and monotone risk for optimally tuned ridge (isotropic prior) are side observations.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies asymptotic and finite-sample linear regression, including PCR and ridgeless estimators, rather than deep-network scaling or training-time sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Risk-curve behavior depends on the relation between feature covariance and coefficient prior: the paper distinguishes aligned, misaligned, and random relations, and states PCR monotonicity under a decreasing conditional signal-strength relation.

fits_no_version.finding: The optimal ridge parameter is negative in the overparameterized regime when Σx and Σβ are aligned and SNR is high. This is read as implicit ℓ2 regularization from overparameterization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overparameterization acts as implicit ℓ2 regularization, so the optimal explicit ridge penalty can be negative when p>n.

record.problems: The central theory relies on stated covariance and boundedness assumptions. Several plotted curve values are not numerically reported, and no uncertainty intervals or error bars are given. The results cover linear regression settings rather than deep networks.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. Risk comparisons across different λ or weighting matrices were omitted because they compare regularization choices rather than testing the listed double-descent versions.

untested.parts: The unregularized or ridgeless sample-size sweep near the threshold is not reported. Only the optimally tuned ridge case is analyzed.
No single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
The role of label noise in driving the peak is not tested. The disappearance of the peak under optimal ridge is shown only for an isotropic prior; the anisotropic Σβ case is left as future work.
There is no re-indexing by an effective number of parameters.

missing.what: Ridgeless risk versus optimally regularized risk as γ varies. Optimal ridge gives 'considerable improvement' over ridgeless, growing with γ and with the condition number. This bears on V6's regularization dependence.

record.verdict_notes: These are theoretical linear-regression results with small finite-sample simulations and no error bars. R6 was relinked from V4 to V6/V3, because optimal ridge is not an interpolating estimator. In ridgeless regression, raising γ also changes the true coefficient dimension, a caveat the authors note. The Figure 9 curves cannot be read numerically.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses linear regression, not deep networks, and does not test model-wise double descent in deep networks.
It does not measure test error over training epochs.
It does not vary training sample count near the interpolation threshold to test whether adding samples raises test error.
The study tests linear-regression settings, not all model classes; it does not establish a universal curve across model classes.
It does not test whether a single effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.

Although noise and regularization appear in the analysis, the study does not test whether label noise drives double-descent peaks, whether peaks split for that reason, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes them.
It does not compare the second descent with a curve indexed by an effective number of parameters.

rows.subject: principal component regression (PCR) estimator
rows.operation_detail: Varied the fraction θ of leading covariance eigenvectors retained and analyzed prediction risk as θγ crosses 1.

conditions.value: E[g|h] decreasing; h has continuous p.d.f.

rows.value: The paper states that risk has a spike as θγ → 1− and then decreases as θ increases further; under the stated decreasing E[g|h] condition, risk is decreasing in θ when θγ > 1.
rows.note: The authors describe this as confirming double descent for PCR under more general covariance and signal settings than prior work.

rows.subject: principal component regression (PCR) estimator
rows.operation_detail: Varied retained PCR fraction θ and plotted prediction risk.
rows.note: The text says PCR risk is largely decreasing with θ, especially in the misaligned case, while also noting that the plotted PCR risk is not always monotone for θγ > 1. The plotted values are not reported numerically.
rows.check: The condition should cover all three covariance relations, not only misaligned. The caption says PCR risk is largely decreasing, especially when misaligned. The non-monotone 'blue curve' is not identified as misaligned; the misaligned case is the one called decreasing.

source_check.correct: For the nonmonotonicity result, broaden the condition to the aligned, other and misaligned covariance settings compared in Figure 9(b). The caption identifies a nonmonotone blue curve without identifying its covariance relation in the extracted text. Section 4 explicitly describes overparameterized PCR risk as monotonically decreasing in the misaligned case; that restricted result supports V4 and warrants observed rather than partial.

rows.subject: ridgeless regression estimator
rows.operation_detail: Varied the dimension ratio γ and plotted prediction risk.
rows.value: The text reports multiple peaks in the overparameterized regime, especially when Σx and Σβ are misaligned.
rows.note: The text attributes the multiple peaks to anisotropic covariances. Numerical values are shown only in the plot.
rows.check: For V6, the multiple peaks are observed, but the paper attributes them to anisotropic covariances, not label noise. For V4, risk does not simply improve past interpolation: several peaks appear as γ grows beyond 1. So the V4 state is partial, not observed.

source_check.correct: Use version-specific states: V4 partial, because additional post-interpolation peaks qualify a simple descending branch; V6 observed for its multiple-descent component. The paper attributes these peaks to anisotropic covariances, especially misalignment.

rows.subject: optimally tuned ridge regression estimator (Σw = I)
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed optimally regularized prediction risk as a function of γ.
rows.value: The risk is an increasing function of γ ∈ (0, ∞).
rows.note: The authors interpret the result as saying that, under proper regularization, increasing training data size helps. As a dimension-ratio sweep, it reports no second descent for this specified optimally tuned ridge setting.
rows.check: This row is mislinked to V4. Optimally tuned ridge does not interpolate, so it is not a test of V4's second descent. Risk rising monotonically in γ over (0,∞) means no peak at γ=1. For V6 this is the predicted disappearance under optimal regularization. For V3, the authors read it as more data always helping. The state is absent with respect to the peak or harm effect, not reversed.

source_check.correct: Use version-specific states: V6 observed for peak removal under optimal regularization; V3 reversed, because increasing training data helps under the stated assumptions. Proposition 7 gives increasing risk in γ over (0,∞), with λopt = γσ̃²/c and E[β*β*ᵀ] = (c/p)I.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5, risk-monotonicity discussion and Proposition 7, lines 736–751.
source_check.problem: Absent cannot describe both linked versions: peak removal supports V6, while monotone improvement with more data opposes the V3 effect.

tranche.reason: The study derives prediction-risk results using generalized linear regression and PCR, providing a different method addressing double descent and regularization.

source_check.notes: Figure 9's extracted text does not identify the covariance relation of the nonmonotone blue PCR curve. The optimal-ridge monotonicity theorem assumes an isotropic signal prior; the paper explicitly leaves general anisotropic priors unresolved.

statements.correction: V4 label for this study: limits_scope. Figure 9(a): multiple overparameterized peaks under anisotropic covariances, especially misalignment. Figure 9(b): PCR risk need not be monotone for θγ>1; misaligned PCR is described as monotonically decreasing in Section 4.
statements.problem: The descriptions of anisotropic multiple descent and finite-sample PCR nonmonotonicity are supported. For this study, the challenges label overstates the evidence: additional peaks qualify sustained improvement without establishing that renewed descent is absent.
